# Uniform control of the small-slope boundary for diagonal kernels

Fix an integer d>=2. Write t=1/(d+1), theta=d/(d+1), and Gamma=theta^d.
For0<a<=1 and0<=beta<=at define the exact diagonal-envelope deficit
D(a,beta) as in `candidate a38c69b78fd106d1`.
This note concerns this explicit scalar deficit, not the general OC
depth functional.

The sole scalar input used below is

    f(v)+f(-v)>=2+theta v^2,  0<=v<=1,
    f(v)=(1+v)^(d+1)/(1+theta v)^d,                      (S)

with strict inequality for v>0. This is proved, with the stronger
quartic remainder theta*v^4/4, in
`candidate 31c8bae81eb26cc3`; its full
independent root audit is `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
The expansion and all uniform estimates below are proved independently
of that scalar argument.

## 1. A uniform quadrature identity

Let g be continuous with compact support on[0,infinity), piecewise C^2,
and with right derivative of bounded variation. For any a>0,

    sum_(h>=0) g(ah) = (1/a) integral_0^infinity g(x)dx
                         +g(0)/2+E_a(g),
    |E_a(g)| <= (a/8) Var(g').                          (1)

To prove this, on each interval[ha,(h+1)a], integrate twice by parts
with the nonnegative kernel(x-ha)((h+1)a-x)/2. The trapezoid difference
is the integral of this kernel against the distributional derivative
of g'. This includes all derivative jumps. Its absolute value is at
most(a^2/8) times the variation of g' on that interval. Sum the
finitely many nonzero intervals, use telescoping endpoint weights,
and divide by a. This proves(1), including knots in interval interiors.

## 2. The exact scaled kernels

Put v=beta/(at) in[0,1] and x=ah. After division by Gamma, the left
and right envelope terms are exactly

    L_v(x)=(1-vx)^(d-1)[1-(d+1-dv)x]_+,
    R_(a,v)(x)=(1+av+vx)^(d-1)
                         [1-dav-(d+1+dv)x]_+.          (2)

Define each expression as zero beyond the support of its positive
part. On their active intervals the first factors are nonnegative.
For0<=a<=1/(2d),0<=v<=1 these functions have support in[0,1].
On their active intervals they are polynomials of degree d whose
coefficients range over a compact set. Their first derivatives have
at most one jump, at the final endpoint. Consequently

    Var(L_v'), Var(R_(a,v)') <= C_d                      (3)

for one finite constant depending only on d. This follows directly
by bounding the polynomial first and second derivatives on[0,1]
and adding the endpoint derivative jump. No differentiability of a
selected truncation index is used. The mass function m(x)=(1-x)_+^d
has the same properties. Equation(1) therefore applies UNIFORMLY
to all these functions.

## 3. Smooth dependence of the right integral

Let I_R(a,v)=integral R_(a,v), and put

    A=1-dav,  B=d+1+dv,  C=1+av.

Changing variables x=(A/B)y on its active interval gives the finite
formula

    I_R(a,v)=(A^2/B) sum_(j=0)^(d-1)
       binom(d-1,j) C^(d-1-j)(vA/B)^j/[(j+1)(j+2)].     (4)

It follows by expanding(C+vAy/B)^(d-1) and integrating y^j(1-y).
On0<=a<=1/(2d),0<=v<=1, A>=1/2 and B>=d+1, so(4) has bounded
first and second a-derivatives uniformly on this compact rectangle.
Taylor's theorem thus proves

    I_R(a,v)=I_R(0,v)+a J_d(v)+O_d(a^2),                (5)

where J_d(v)=partial_a I_R(0,v) is continuous and J_d(0)=0. The latter
identity is immediate because(4) is independent of a when v=0.
The notation O_d here means an absolute bound by one fixed
dimension-dependent constant on the WHOLE specified rectangle.

Also L_v(0)=1 and
R_(a,v)(0)=(1+av)^(d-1)(1-dav)=1+O_d(a) uniformly.
Applying(1) to the two kernels, using(3)-(5), gives

    sum_h [L_v(ah)+R_(a,v)(ah)]
      =[I_L(v)+I_R(0,v)]/a+J_d(v)+1+O_d(a),            (6)

where I_L(v)=integral L_v. The mass identity is

    sum_h(1-ah)_+^d=1/[a(d+1)]+1/2+O_d(a).             (7)

## 4. The continuous deficit and its strict gap

Direct integration of(2) at a=0 yields, for v>0,

    I_L(v)+I_R(0,v)=[f(v)+f(-v)-2]/(d v^2).             (8)

For example, setting A=d+1-dv and B=(d+1)(1-v) in the left
integral and substituting y=1-vx gives

    I_L(v)=[A/(d+1)-B/d+B^(d+1)/(d(d+1)A^d)]/v^2.

The right integral is the same expression with v replaced by-v.
Adding them gives(8). At v=0 each integral is1/[2(d+1)], so the
sum extends continuously with value1/(d+1). This also follows
directly from the compactly supported continuous integrands.

Define

    G_d(v)=I_L(v)+I_R(0,v)-1/(d+1).

Under(S), G_d is continuous, nonnegative, and strictly positive for
v>0. Combining(6)-(8) with the definition of the exact deficit gives
the uniform expansion

    D(a,atv)/Gamma
       =-G_d(v)/a-J_d(v)-1/2+O_d(a).                   (9)

This identity retains the discrete endpoint correction and the
right-fiber shift beta. Omitting either would change the constant term.

## 5. No positive maximum escapes to zero slope

Under(S),

    limsup_(a down to0, 0<=beta<=at) D(a,beta)
                                      <=-Gamma/2.     (10)

Here the limsup ranges over ALL simultaneous choices of beta. To
verify it, take any such sequence and pass to a subsequence on which
v=beta/(at) converges. If its limit is positive, continuity and
strict positivity give G_d(v)>=c>0 eventually. The bounded J_d and
uniform remainder in(9) force D to minus infinity. If v tends to
zero, discard the nonpositive term-G_d(v)/a. Continuity gives
J_d(v)->0, and(9) yields limsup D/Gamma<=-1/2. These two cases prove
(10); no rate assumption relating v and a is needed.

In particular there is an epsilon_d>0 such that every0<a<epsilon_d
has D(a,beta)<0 throughout the permitted tilt interval. On the other
hand the explicit pair a=2/(d+1), beta=1/[d(d+1)] has strictly
positive deficit Gamma sum_(h>=1)(1-2h/(d+1))_+^d. Thus the global
maximum of D is attained on a compact set away from a=0. The audited
compact double-knot reduction can then place a maximum at one of its
integer pairs H,J. This does NOT compare those pairs or identify
the sharp maximum; that remains a separate arithmetic problem.

## 6. Explicit quantitative exclusion of the small-slope edge

The independent full audit
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)` supplies
explicit estimates, including the moving-endpoint term in the second
derivative of the right integral. Write

    V_d=3d(3d+1)2^(d-3),
    T_d=2^(d-3)(9d^2-7d+2)/(d+1),
    E_d=(d+2)2^(d-4),
    C_d=V_d/4+d/8+T_d/2+E_d,
    K_d=d(2d+1)/(d+1)^2 [1+1/(d+1)]^(d-2).

On the full rectangle 0<=a<=1/(2d), 0<=v<=1, the absolute remainder
in (9) is at most C_d a and |J_d(v)|<=K_d v. The stronger scalar
inequality gives G_d(v)>=v^2/[4(d+1)]. Completing the square yields

    D(a,atv)/Gamma
      <=-1/2-v^2/[4(d+1)a]+K_d v+C_d a
      <=-1/2+[C_d+(d+1)K_d^2]a.

Consequently the explicit positive cutoff

    epsilon_d=min{1/(2d),1/[4(C_d+(d+1)K_d^2)]}

satisfies D(a,beta)<=-Gamma/4 for every 0<a<=epsilon_d and
0<=beta<=at. The cited audit proves each constant directly; the root
has independently read and verified those derivative and variation
estimates. This quantitative version strengthens the attainment
conclusion but does not compare the remaining double knots.
